and Punarvasu are prescribed for the rite of shaving, provided they are in conjunction with an auspicious rising sign and possess favorable stars.

it destroys longevity when performed for Mars; and it destroys everything when performed for Saturn.

On Thursday, by performing one hundred thousand recitations, there is the attainment of general excellence.

The tonsure ceremony (cuḍākarma). [It is performed] on the third day after the birth, or on a day when the moon enters a favorable constellation, and so forth.

The commencement of learning should take place under the seven asterisms beginning with Rohiṇī (the "lotus-born" group), under the three asterisms beginning with Hasta, under Maitra (Anurādhā), Uttarāṣāḍhā, and the Purvas; it may also be undertaken under Revatī, Mūla, and Ārdrā during the bright fortnight.
At the commencement of learning, Jupiter is most excellent; the Sun and Mars are middling;
Saturn and Mars [in conjunction] cause death; and Mercury and the Moon result in ignorance.
The hair, the flower, the stone, the great consciousness, the self, the dawn, the three, the smoke, the three, the delight.

May you take pleasure in these [words]; may they be favorable to us. O Vāra, Budha, Vṛṣabhin, Ācaṃśa, Madhyama, and Amateva!

Regarding marriage: it is auspicious on a lunar day (tithi) presided over by Jupiter, Brahmā (Jupiter), Anurādhā, Aśvinī, Venus, the Sun, Vāyu (Svātī), Varuṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), Hari (Śravaṇa), and Tvaṣṭṛ (Citrā). It is also auspicious when the Sun has entered Aquarius or Virgo, during a favorable moment (lagna), and on days ruled by Venus, Jupiter, or Mars. Nine days [are recommended].
The bride's entry into the community is auspicious.
One should perform the formal acceptance (*parigraha*) of the fire on the days of Mṛgaśīrṣa, Puṣya, Aśvinī, Svāti, Śravaṇā, and Vāruṇa; during the journeys of a new bride;

on days that are auspicious for play; and under the asterisms of Pauṣṇa, Prajāpati, Puṣya, the three *Uttara*s, and Śakra (Jyeṣṭhā), as well as those belonging to Soma and the common (*sādhāraṇa*) ones.

On the third lunar day (tithi) of the bright fortnight in the months of Pauṣa,
Caitra, or Māgha, under the asterisms of Puṣya, Aśvinī, Śravaṇa, Svātī, or Jyeṣṭhā, and on a Monday, Wednesday, or Saturday, the divine [initiation] is indeed highly commended. Furthermore,
when the planets are auspicious and free from planetary conflicts (vāra-śatru-virodhana), it is always conducive to sovereignty and glory.

O King, regarding the grace of the king at the commencement of a marriage, when all Brahmins are present and acting according to his command, there is no need to consider the qualities of the lunar mansions; it is merely a matter of custom.

The Aśvinī, Revatī, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Puṣya, and Jyeṣṭhā are for the highest journey. Rohiṇī, the three Pūrvās (Pūrvaphalgunī, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, and Pūrvabhādrapadā), Svātī, Anurādhā, and the asterism of Varuṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), as well as Śravaṇā and Dhaniṣṭhā, are remembered as the intermediate group.

and when that time of dawn bestows the fruit of an increase in wealth and grain, it is praised as "godhulikā."

Of [the planet] Jupiter: Bṛhaspati, Soma-mitra, Sudhā-dṛṣṭi, Vidāvara, Vācaspati, Vāgīśa, Nītijña, and Jñātivardhana. (16a)
I am the living soul, Aṅgiras, the wise one, the one clad in yellow garments, and the Grandfather.
The best of gods, the lord of the gods, with a golden body and the luster of saffron;
the master of speech, worthy of worship by the gods, the one honored by the gods, and adored by the thirty deities.
A skilled minister, a master of ritual conduct, a knower of the Vedas, a preceptor, and a poet [are the qualities] of Bṛhaspati.
Bhṛguja, Bhṛguputra, Bhṛgusunu, Bhṛgu, and Kavi [are synonyms for Śukra].
The minister of the Daityas, the one worshipped by the Daityas, the presiding lord of the Daityas, and the preceptor of the Asuras.
Uśanas Bhārgava, the son of Kavi, Śukra, was the domestic priest of the Daityas.
The author of Āsphujit-kāvya was a knower of mantras, the best among those who possess mantra-knowledge.
Of Śukra: Śauri, Manda, Sūryaputra, Chāyāputra, Śanaiścara, Asitāmbaradhara, Pātālāṅga, Kāla, and Pañcaśikha. Of Śanaiścara: 7.
Tamas, Gura, Asura, Rāhu, Surāri, and Siṃhikāsuta.
The Daitya Upaplava, the eclipser of the moon and sun, fell down.
16b) Of Rāhu: || 8 || The comet Śikhī, the son of Brahmā, is established as being of smoky color.
*Ketoḥ*. Thus are the names of the nine planets. *Aśvayuk*, *turaṅga*, *vājī*, *ghoṭaka*, and *raṅgama* [are synonyms for horse].
Aśvovāha, Raṅga, Hayada, and Aśvinī likewise.
Of Aśvinī: Yamontaka, Pretapati, and Kṛtānta; likewise, Bharaṇī.
Yama, Capala, Rātri, Īśa, and Mātṛ are likewise the presiding deities of Bharaṇī.
Hutasana, Śikhāvat, Bahuruci, Ahnara, Anala,
Vṛhadbhānu, Kṛśānu, Pāvaka, and Havyavāhana.
Dahana, ukta, taptu, kuvaṇhi, vītihotra, dhanañjaya, vaiśvānara, varhiṣṭha, śūṣma, śociṣkeśa, and uṣarbudha.
Rohitāśva, Vāyu, Sakhā, Jātavedas, Tanūnapāt, Kṛṣṇavartman, Jvalana, Agni, Āśuśukṣaṇi, and Kṛttikā. [These are] of Kṛttikā.
Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, Lokeśa, Rohiṇī, Kamalāsana, Viśvākṣa, Viśvakartṛ, Padmayoni, and Prajāpati.
Four-faced and four-mouthed, Brahmā is born from the lotus;
he is the Supreme Lord, the best of heroes, Viriñci, and the Grandfather.
Brahmā, Vedhā, Vidhi, Sraṣṭṛ, Svayambhū, Caturānana, Hiraṇyagarbha, Avjayoni, Ātmabhū, Devanāyaka.
In Rohiṇī: Mṛgaśīrṣa, Mṛgaśiras, Mṛgāṅka, Rohiṇīdhava, Oṣadhīśa, Niśānātha, Niśākara, and Niśāpati.
The moon is Akroja, Atrika, Soma, Indu, Kumuda-bandhu,
Śītaraśmi, Sudhāraśmi, Himaraśmi, and Kalānidhi.
Vidhu, Sudhāṃśu, Śubhrāṃśu, Himāṃśu, Kṣapākara, Śiśirāṃśu, Śaśadhara, Rātri, and Rajanipati.
The gentle one, the moon, the king of the twice-born, the hare-marked one, and the one with cool rays; [these are the names] of Mṛgaśiras.
Ārdrā, Raudra, Nīlakaṇṭha, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Girijāpati.
Īśvara, Īśa, Īśāna, Mahādeva, and Maheśvara.
Caṇḍīśa, Tryambaka, Bhargava, Śaṅkara, Candraśekhara, Virūpākṣa, Śiva, Śūlin, Pinākin, and Pramathādhipa.
Hara, the destroyer of Smara, the auspicious one, the Lord of Beings, the husband of Pārvatī,
Paśupati, Vāmadeva, the Lord of Umā, and the destroyer of the three cities.
Kṛśānuretās, Sarvajña, Dhūrjati, and Nīlalohita [are the forms] of Ārdrā.
Aditi, the mother of the gods, and Devāmā, as well as Punarvasu; [the constellation] of Punarvasu.
Vācaspati, Tiṣya, Puṣpa, Devamantrin, Kavi—these are the names by which he is remembered; Surapūjya, Surādhyakṣa, and Surācārya are the names of Bṛhaspati.
Born from Śikhaṇḍin, he is the best of gods, the subduer of speech, and the teacher of the twice-born.
Aṅgiras, Śukra, Vāgīśa, Vākpati, the one worshipped by the thirty gods, Somamitra, Sudhādṛṣṭi, Hemāṅga,
and Kuṅkumacchavi— these are the names of Puṣpa.

Aśleṣā is the Tuja, the Nāga, the serpent, the lord of snakes, the one dwelling in the sand, the one with eyes on its ears, the bearer of poison, the one with tusks like a boar, and the one that moves by coiling.
Kuṇḍalī, guṇapāt, sarpa, cakrī, vyāla, sarīsṛpa,
āśīviṣadhara, bhogī, jihmaga, pavanāśana, kākodara, dīrghapṛṣṭha, viṣāgni, pannaga, uraga— these are the names of Aśleṣā.
The ancestors are his deity; he is constantly [worshipping] the Maghās. Of the Maghās.
The womb is the remainder that bestows happiness.

The region known as Bhaga is the location of fat (medas), and it is indeed Pūrvaphalgunī; this is remembered by the wise as the gate for the exit of the embryo and the knot of the womb. [This refers to] Pūrvaphalgunī.
Having known this, one should worship another [deity] during the Uttaraphalgunī [nakṣatra]. [This concludes the section on] Uttaraphalgunī.
Hastārka, Satavitā, Sūrya, Āditya, Nanātha, Divākara,
Bhāskara, Ahaskara, Dineśa, and Dineśvara.
Niśāntaka, Niśāri, Tapana, Savitṛ, Āravi,
Virocana, Citrabhānu, Mārtaṇḍa, and likewise Mihira.
The hot-rayed one, the sharp-rayed one, the lord of splendors, the lord of the day,
the thousand-rayed one, the harsh-rayed one, the sun-jewel, and the sovereign of the day.
Bhāsvat, Vivasvat, Saptāśva, Pūṣan, Āditya, Prabhākara,
Mātariśvan, Haridaśva, Dvādaśātmā, and Vikartana.
Vibhāvasu (the Sun), Grahapati (Mars), and Surasamārūṇa (Mercury) are the lords of Hasta. Tvaṣṭṛ is the lord of Citrā. [The lord] of Citrā is Tvaṣṭṛ.
Sarvagati, Āsurī, Anila, as well as Pavana, Pāvamāna, Vāta, and Pavamānadaivata;
The wind is called *vāta*, *sparśana*, *vāyu*, *mātariśvan*, and *sadāgati*;
it is also known as *gaṃdhavāha*, *gaṃdhavāha*, *marut*, *māruta*, and *samīraṇa*.
Nabhasvat, Sthāṇu, Sanasvāti, Jagatprāṇa, and Prabhañjana are the [deities] of Svātī. Svātyāḥ.
Rāva, Viśākhā, Śakra-Agni, and likewise Indra-Agni; [these are] of Viśākhā.
Anurādhā is remembered as friendly; Viśākha is remembered as its younger brother. [This concerns] Anurādhā.
Jyeṣṭha, Surādhipa, Vajrī, Puruhūta, and Purandara.
Surāsīra, Sahasrākṣa, Vāsava, and Pākaśāsana.
Lord of the Suras, destroyer of Vṛtra, O Excellent Night, Lord of Śacī;
he who is heard by the aged, born from the waters, Maghavat, and whose vehicle is the clouds.
Vāstoṣpati, the lord of the gods, the protector of the quarters,
the slayer of Jambha, the one with bay horses, the possessor of the Maruts, and the destroyer of Suviṣu.
Indra, Śakra, Śatamanyu, Jiṣṇu, Lekharṣabha, Ākhaṇḍala, Duścyavana, Svārāt, Namuci, and Sudana— these are the names from Jyāṣṭhā.
The Āsarasas have Karvuru as their root; those belonging to the Nairṛta region are the Rāśaryas.
The sage sat down upon a rākṣasa who was prowling about at night.
May the Yātudhāna, the Puṇyajana, the Kravyāda, and likewise the Krośapa [be destroyed]. [This is] for the root.
Salila, jīvana, and pātha are the names for water; Pūrvāṣāḍhā is called "water-named. [These are the qualities] of Pūrvāṣāḍhā.
Viśvākṛt is Uttarāṣāḍhā; he is called Viśvadeva [in relation] to Uttarāṣāḍhā.
Dāmodara, Padmanābha, Keśava, he whose banner bears Garuḍa;
Varāha, Puṇḍarīkākṣa, Nṛsiṃha, the slayer of the Daityas.
Govinda is indeed Acyuta, Kṛṣṇa is indeed Ananta, and he is indeed unconquered.
Adhokṣaja, born of the world, is the agent of creation, preservation, and destruction.
Viṣṇu is without beginning or end, the teacher of the three worlds, and the one of mighty strides;
he is Nārāyaṇa, four-armed, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Clad in yellow garments, the conqueror of Kaiṭabha, adorned with a forest garland;
he who bears the Śrīvatsa mark, the father of the universe, the Lord of Śrī, and likewise the bearer of Śrī.
Hari, Śruti, Vaikuṇṭha, Hṛṣīkeśa, Janārdana, Devakīnandana, Śauri, Śravaṇa, and Puruṣottama.
The sustainer of the universe, the creator of the universe, the enemy of Kaṃsa, the slayer of Madhu,
the lord of Lakṣmī, the foe of the demon Madhu, the one who has no enemies, and the maker of all worlds.
The destroyer of the hosts of Dānavas and Alīns, Cakrapāṇi, Mādhava,
likewise the younger brother of Indra, Svabhū, and he who is marked with the Śrīvatsa— these are [the forms] of Śravaṇā.
And Dhaneṣṭhā is Dhanavasu; [the hymn] of Dhaneṣṭhā.
The lord of waters named Varuṇa arises from Śatabhiṣā; he is Pracetas, Varuṇa, the noose-wielder, and the protector of aquatic creatures. [In the asterism] Śatabhiṣā.
Ajaikapād is Proṣṭhapada; it is Pūrvabhādrapadā according to the wise. [This refers to] Pūrvabhādrapadā.
And Uttarabhādrapadā is said to be Ahivṛdhna; [this refers to] Uttarabhadrā.
The end of the asterism is Revatī, Pauṣṇa, and Pūṣan; this is also its name. [This refers to] Revatī.
Thus end the names of the lunar mansions.
Vibhava, Prīti, Āyuṣmān, Saubhāgya, and Śobhana; likewise Atigaṇḍa, Sukarman, Dhṛti, and Śūla.
Gata, Vṛddhi, and Druva have been explained, as well as Harṣaṇa; then Vaja, Śuddhi, Vyatīpāta, Variyān, Parigha, Śiva, Siddhi, Sādhya, Śubha, Śukla,
Brahma, Aindra, and Dhṛti.
Twenty-seven [deities] are declared; they should be consumed as their fruits are equal to their names.
Thus are the names of yoga.
Vava, Vālava, Kaulava, Taitila,
Gara, Vaṇija, and Viṣṭi— these seven are the movable (cara) karaṇas.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, Śakuni is in the western petal;
Catuṣpāda and Nāga shall be in both petals of the new moon.
And on the first lunar day (pratipad) of the bright fortnight, Kintughna is in the first petal;
the wise have declared these four to be fixed karaṇas.
And at the end of the first tithi of the bright fortnight, the Karaṇa called Vava occurs; the remaining [Karaṇas] beginning with Vava are determined by dividing [the lunar days] by seven.
Thus end the names of the instruments.
The Rudras, Ādityas, Vasus, Varuṇa, Viśvedevas, Vidhātṛ, Vidhi, Śatakratu, Puruhūta, Vahni,
Naktamcara, Aryaman, and the Yonis— these fifteen muhūrtas are said to belong to the day.
The names of the divisions of the day.
The Muhūrtas of the night are Giri, Sāja, Pāda, Hivvudhna, Pūṣā, Ciya, Mā,
Agni, Vidhātṛ, Candra, Aditi, Jīva, Viṣṇu, Tīkṣṇadyuti, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Samīraṇa.
Thus ends [the section] named "The Muhūrta of Night."
Aries is the first house, Taurus is the second, Gemini is the third,

Cancer is the fourth, Leo is the fifth, Virgo is the sixth, Libra is the seventh, Scorpio is the eighth, Sagittarius is the ninth, Capricorn is the tenth, Aquarius is the eleventh, and Pisces is the twelfth.
Leo, Aquarius, and Aries are the signs of the Lion; Virgo and Pisces are said to be the two of the Provisions; Libra is called the Weigher of Cotton.
Kīṭāli, Vṛścika, Kaurpi, Kodaṇḍa, Tauli, Kodhanu, Ākokera,
Mṛgāsya, Kamaloda, and Somṛga.
The signs are Leo, Aquarius, Pisces, and Aries; these are their names in brief.
One should indicate other synonymous terms for these as they are well-known in common usage.
Thus are the names of the zodiac signs.
Nindamandira, harya, gṛha, veśman, niketana, nilaya, bhavana, āgāra, geha, and hemapadmani are synonyms for "house. Kesana means "hair."
Thus end the names of houses.

The six seasons, beginning with Capricorn and the others, are the enjoyment of the Sun by the two-fold consciousness; they are Śiśira, Vasanta, Grīṣma, Śarad, likewise Hemanta, and the sixth is named [Śiśira].
Thus are the names of the six seasons.
Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, and the first quarter of Kṛttikā—this is the field of Aṅgāraka (Mars), which is ordained as the sign of Aries. || 1 ||
Three quarters of Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, and half of Mṛgaśiras should be known as the field of Śukra; it is ordained as the sign of Taurus (Vṛṣa). || 2 ||
The half of Mṛgaśiras, Ārdrā, and three quarters of Punarvasu should be known as the domain of Mercury; it is called the zodiac sign of Gemini. || 3 ||
One quarter of Punarvasu together with Puṣya and Āśleṣā should be known as the lunar field (candrakṣetra); it is called the zodiac sign of Cancer (karkaṭa). || 4 ||
Maghā, Pūrvaphalgunī, and Uttaraphalgunī should be known as the solar domain;
it is ordained that the Leo zodiac sign (siṃharāśi) corresponds to this. || 5 ||
The three quarters of Uttarāṣāḍhā, Hasta, half of Citrā, and Maitra (Anurādhā) should be known as the domain of Mercury; it is ordained as the sign of Virgo (Kanyā). || 6 ||
The half of Citrā conjoined with Svātī and the three quarters of Viśākhā should be known as the solar domain (sūryakṣetra); it is prescribed as the zodiac sign of Libra (tulārāśi). || 7 ||
One quarter of Viśākhā, along with Anurādhā and Jyeṣṭhā, should be known as the domain of Mars; it is prescribed that this constitutes the sign of Scorpio. || 8 ||
Mūla, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, and Uttarāṣāḍhā should be known as the field of Jīva; it is ordained that the sign of Sagittarius (Dhanu) is [the domain] of the Moon. || 9 ||
The three quarters of Uttarā-bhadrapadā, Śravaṇa, and half of Dhaniṣṭhā are to be known as the domain of Śauri (Saturn); this is declared to be the sign of Capricorn.
The half of Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣā, and the first three [asterisms] of Pūrvabhādrapadā are to be known as the field of Śauri; it is ordained as the sign of Aquarius (Kumbha). || 11 ||
One quarter of Pūrvabhādrapadā and likewise Uttarābhādrapadā and Revatī should be known as the field of Jupiter;
it is ordained as the sign of Pisces.
The names of the Indrarāśi.
The wise know that Aries and Taurus belong to Mars and Venus; Libra and Taurus to Mercury;
Virgo and Gemini to the Moon; Leo and Scorpio to the Sun; Sagittarius and Pisces to Jupiter; and Capricorn and Aquarius to Saturn.
Thus the sages understand the lords of the signs.
Thus are the names of the planetary fields.
I shall state the names of the months: Caitra is called Madhu and Caitraka; Vaiśākha is known as Vaisākha and Mādhava; Jyeṣṭha is likewise Śukra and Śuci.
Āṣāḍha is known as Śrāvaṇika, and Śrāvaṇa is remembered as Nabhas; Nabhasya is Bhādrapada, which is likewise called Bhādra and Proṣṭhapada.
Aśvayuja and Āśvina, Kārttika and Mārgaśīrṣa, Pauṣa and Taiṣa, Sahasya and Tapas, Māgha and Phālguna.
The son of Tapati is Phalguna, who is white, endowed with bright moonlight;
he is dark when mixed with darkness, and these two fortnights are the bright and the dark.
Thus are the names of the months.
Vahni is prescribed for the first lunar day, Prajāpati for the second,
Girijā for the third, and Vighneśa for the fourth.
The fifth is likewise the Nāgas, the sixth is the Son of the Mountain-Dweller (Śiva),
the seventh is the Lord of Day (the Sun), and on the eighth is Maheśvara.
Durgādevī on the ninth day, and likewise Antaka on the tenth.
On the eleventh day, Viśvedeva is the deity; on the twelfth day, likewise, Candra is the deity.
Kāmadeva is the presiding deity of the thirteenth lunar day (tithi), Maheśvara of the fourteenth, and likewise Soma of the full moon; these are the presiding deities of the lunar days.
Thus are the names of the lunar days (tithis).
Likewise, one should always perform the rites concerning the site, the ritual manual, the field, and so forth, for Nandā, during festivals of various splendors.
Marriage, the wearing of new clothes, travel on foot or by carriage, auspicious rites, and acts that promote prosperity [should be undertaken].
Victory is attained in battle for one who employs the yoga of power; indeed, all undertakings that have been commenced are accomplished.
On the Riktā lunar days, there is success in lightning, killing, binding, striking, poison, fire, weapons, and so forth.

One should always perform the rites of fullness, auspiciousness, marriage processions, nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), and pacification (*śāntika*); likewise, the ancestral rites (*pitṛkarma*) on the new moon day, and other auspicious and propitious acts such as the offering of firebrands (*ulkā*).
In the bright fortnight, one should avoid the pair of lunar days (the 2nd and 4th, etc. and the ninth; in the dark fortnight, one should avoid the second and the tenth.
Among those remaining, the even-numbered days are considered excellent, while the odd ones—excluding the ninth—are declared by the lords of sages to be inauspicious.
Just as on the first day of the lunar fortnight when the moon has vanished, the Moon-god should never perform a meager offering with two teeth;
for by doing so, he does not obtain prosperity, but rather swiftly incurs the ruin of his lineage, his kin, and his people.
The tenth lunar day destroys the daughter of one who has bathed; the thirteenth destroys his wealth; and the second destroys both of these as well.
A person desiring prosperity on the seventh, the full moon, the ninth, or the new moon day should never bathe with *amlaka* fruits.
One should avoid oil on the sixth lunar day, shaving on the eighth, and likewise the performance of hair-cutting on the fourteenth.

On the eighth lunar day and subsequent days, one desiring higher rebirth should never eat [meat]; alternatively, on those days, one should respectively consume the skull, weapons, nails, skin, and sesame seeds.
He who performs a marriage on the new moon day, during the *amāvāsyā*, when the lunar mansion is *sūrikta* and the *karana* is named *viṣṭi*,
goes swiftly to the abode of Yama.
The Uttarās, Bharaṇī, the three Pūrvās,

Jyeṣṭhā, Āśleṣā, Viśākhā, Mūla, Varuṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), Aśvinī, Agni (Kṛttikā), Citrā, and Maghā are declared by the sages, according to the force of their sequence, to belong to the gods, humans, and Rākṣasas respectively.
The goat is associated with Citrā and Revatī; the serpent with Āśleṣā, Mṛgaśiras, and Rohiṇī;
the rat with Mūla and Ārdrā; and the mouse with Maghā and the two Phalgunīs.
The Cat, the Well-established, Aśleṣā, Punarvasu, Dhaniṣṭhā, Bhadrapadā, Siṃha, Go, Rūpa,
and the three Uttarās.
The buffalo is under Hasta and Svātī; the four-limbed [elephant] under Varuṇa (Śatabhiṣaj) and Aśvinī; the monkey under Śravaṇa and Āṣāḍhā; and the tigers under Citrā and Viśākhā.
Mṛgaśīrṣa, Jyeṣṭhā, Anurādhā, Revatī, and Bharaṇī are for elephants; Abhijit and Āśleṣā are declared to be the asterisms of the animal kingdom.
Having diligently understood the cow, tiger, elephant, lion, horse, buffalo, snake,
mongoose, rat, man, ram, and likewise the great mouse—
knowing these as the lowest among the worlds— he is always free from sorrow even while serving these two.
When that [sun] is in the asterism Kṛttikā, then it is attained through the merit of the Gajacchāyā Śrāddha.
Where one [tithi] touches the end of two [consecutive] lunar days, if it is a weekday, that is called an *avamadinam* (intercalary day) by the wise;
however, that which occurs when three tithis touch a single day, or when two [tithis] touch two [different] days, is not desired.
When the sun sets after having traversed three muhūrtas of a lunar day (tithi),
those ancient experts in time declare that tithi to be "full" for all religious rites.
Thus ends the section on lunar days.
The horse, the preta, the fire-pit, the fragrant deer, the serpent, the lotus-filled jars, the crow, the buffalo, the two mountains, the elephants,
the variegated peacock, the royal swan (1), the tortoise, the root, the two cotton trees, the man, the *maṭāra*, the *adhaka*, the cow, the pedestal, and the end of the wheel.
Thus has the sequence of the mounts of the stars been described by the wise.
Hasta, Svāti, Mṛgaśiras, Citrā, Puṣya, Jyeṣṭhā, Anurādhā, Āditi (Punarvasu), Ārdrā, and Rohiṇī—
these are the asterisms for the two full-moon nights, Rākā and Anumati, when the moon is visible at night or by day;
otherwise, they are [the other two], Kuhu and Sinīvālī, which are traditionally remembered as the fifteenth days of the dark fortnight when the moon is not seen.
The rules for giving, recitation, and fire-offerings performed on the *kuhū* day yield a hundred thousandfold merit;
even those performed on the *sinīvālī* day yield a thousandfold fruit.

The fifteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha, the thirteenth day of Nabhasya (Śrāvaṇa), the third day of the bright fortnight of Madhava (Vaiśākha), and the ninth day of Urja (Kārttika) are the Yugādi days.
The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvayuja, the twelfth day of Ujjaiḥmadha, the third day [of the same], the third day of Bhādrapada,
and the new moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa.

The eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, the tenth and seventh days of the bright fortnight of Śuci (Jyeṣṭha), the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha, and likewise the full moon days of Nabhasya (Śrāvaṇa), Āṣāḍha, and Kārttika.
The fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, and the full moon days of Caitra and Jyeṣṭha— these fourteen, beginning with Manvantarādi, are declared by the wise to be meritorious.
On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight under the asterism Maghā,
[these] are proclaimed by the sages as bringing success in all undertakings and in accomplishing actions that correspond to one’s own name.
Andhaka, Anumandala, Locana, Madhyalocana, and Surocana; these four types of Rohiṇī and so forth—may they not again appear within this group of asterisms.
If the blind snake (*andhakenika*) is nearby, wealth stolen by thieves is easily recovered; if it is a one-eyed snake (*ibhaka*), it is obtained with effort;

if a flat-nosed snake (*cipiṭabha*), the acquisition of that wealth occurs at a distance and after hearing of it; however, if it is the "excellent-eyed" snake (*uttamavilocanabha*), there is no recovery of the wealth at all.
Punarvasu, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Ārdrā, Jyeṣṭhā,
Anurādhā, Hasta, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā, and Mūla are the constellations that move toward the south.
Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Svātī, Viśākhā,
the two Phalgunīs, Maghā, and the two Bhādrapadas— these nine are the northern-moving constellations.
Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, Puṣya, Citrā, Āśleṣā, Revatī,
Śatabhiṣaj, Dhaniṣṭhā, and Śravaṇa are the nine that move through the middle.
The five asterisms beginning with Vāsava (Dhruva), Uttara, Parā (Punarvasu), and the others,

as well as Rohiṇī along with the three Uttaras, are called "Fixed" (dhruva) by the sages; they are auspicious for those seeking wealth, for sowing seeds, for the consecration of kings, for Rāma-śānti rites, and for other beneficial acts requiring stability.
The asterisms presided over by Tvaṣṭṛ,
Mitra, and the Moon, as well as those ending in 'na' and 'm', are auspicious for the decoration of ornaments and the performance of songs and auspicious rites.
Aśvinī, Gurubha (Pūrvaphalgunī), and the asterism presided over by the Sun (Hasta), along with Abhijit—these four are considered "light" (laghu).
They grant success in meritorious acts, ornamentation, arts, pleasure, medicine, knowledge, crafts, and travel.

By reciting the mantras of Mūla, Śakra, Śiva, Sarpa, and the deities, one is known as "Extremely Sharp" (Atikṣṇa). Furthermore, here [in this practice] are the accomplishment of mantras for spirits (bhūta), yakṣas, and treasures (nidhi), as well as the methods for piercing, binding, and killing.
The wise declare that this group of five movable asterisms— Punarvasu joined with the three Vaiṣṇavas (Anurādhā,
Jyeṣṭhā, and Mūla) and Svāti— is prescribed for the destruction of enemies, the neutralization of poison, breaking bonds, eradication, and [resistance against] weapons and fire.
The fire-god Havyavāha, together with the two deities known as Mitra, brings success in the mixed rite; having abandoned the hand-grasping ceremony, there is indeed the flowering of results.
Neither the conjunctions nor the ascendant, nor the strength of the stars and the moon, nor Jupiter;
neither the yogas nor Rāhu, nor even the [inauspicious] time—none of these can overcome [the effects of] the Puṣpa [yoga].
If the Bhadrātithi occurs when the moon is in an odd-numbered lunar mansion (dhiṣṇya),
how could it not be so on the days of Jupiter, Saturn, and Mars?
This yoga, known as Tripuṣkara, has been proclaimed by the sages;
it yields a threefold fruit when [the victim] is lost, struck down, or likewise dead.

The interval between the asterisms of Pūṣan (Revatī) and Aśvinī, Sārpa (Āśleṣā) and Pitrya (Maghā), and Jyeṣṭhā and Mūla is known as Gaṇḍānta; it lasts for four nāḍikās and is inauspicious during journeys, at the time of birth, and at the time of marriage.

The *gaṇḍānta* of the lunar mansion, the lunar day, and the zodiac sign is traditionally held to be threefold, measuring one, two, and one-and-a-half *ghaṭikās* respectively at the ninth and fourth degrees.
A person born [under a Gaṇḍānta] does not live; the offspring of the mother would fall into the hands of their own family.
If he should live, then in the Gaṇḍānta there will be many elephants and horses, and he shall possess great wealth.
One should avoid concealing one's faults, the cremation of a *preta*, the gathering of wood for execution, and the weaving of hemp.

The measurement of the *tāraka* (the star) is as follows: three peaks (3), three qualities (3), six tastes (6), four senses (4), three fires (3), one moon (1), four Vedas (4), three qualities (3), six seasons (6), five (5), two fortnights (28), four objects of sense (4), one *ka* (1), one moon (1), four elements (4), three oceans (3), three fires (3), eleven Rudras (11), two horses (2), eight Vasus (8), thirty-one fires (31), four elements (4), one hundred (100), two fortnights (2), eight Vasus (8), and thirty-two (32). Thus is the measurement of the *tāraka*.
The duration of the constellations beginning with Aśvinī is measured by their respective number of stars.
Its form is like that of a horse's head, and its shape is like a vulva, resembling a barber’s razor; its head is like a temple, and it is just like that of a deer.
Resembling a jewel, like a pearl, indeed like the moon in the heart, having the luster of a discus, resembling a rampart, a bed, the shape of a hand, and the form of a pearl.
Resembling a jewel, it is like the archway of Mount Māturuṅga.
Even if pierced by a planet, even if joined with inauspicious [planets], even if subject to opposition, or even if retrograde,
[the Moon] certainly fulfills all purposes when worshipped with thousands of white flowers.
The astrologer, dressed in white garments and honored like the moon,
should contemplate, "I am the Moon," and perform [the rite] without sloth.
One who is faithful and composed should recite the mantra with tears;
indeed, one should give a desired sacrificial fee for the pacification of the defects of warts.
Just as terrible serpent venom dissolves through the recollection of mantras,
even so does this fault of the Gaṇas dissolve by means of the prescribed rite.
Being pure, one should give a vessel of refined gold along with copper and sesame seeds to a knower of the Yajurveda, for the sake of pacifying the defects caused by the Gaṇas.
The *puṣya* [nakṣatra] destroys all that is done by others, yet it does not destroy the faults of another;
indeed, even when the moon is in its most beloved *puṣya*, every action performed there always attains success.
Just as the lion is among all four-footed beasts, so too is Puṣpa among the forest-dwelling animals;
even when the moon is in opposition or in its own domain, tasks undertaken under Puṣpa reach their fulfillment.
Even if pierced by a house-planet, the father should abandon the child—who has not yet attained the root-nature—before eight years have passed; otherwise, he should not look upon its face.
Then, having placed [the child] on his lap with its feet downward, he should follow the path of birth as the second father.
In the third house, there is loss of wealth; in the fourth, it brings about happiness.
One born by day kills at night; one born at night perishes during the day; and one born at the time of twilight perishes upon being abandoned.
A newborn child [is likewise lost] through neglect.

In the *Pratiṣamatsya* [Purāṇa], the fruit is said to be exactly that same as in the *Sārpabha*; for the pacification of the aforementioned defects, a propitiatory rite (*śāntika*) should be performed.
With a hundred medicinal roots, earth, mud, gems, auspicious seeds, and jars filled with water and their respective contents;
One who desires prosperity should perform the ritual bath for the mother, father, and children, accompanied by oblations and gifts.
One should fashion a copper vessel weighing sixteen palas,
or eight, or four, or even two, making it very beautiful.
In the center of that, having placed a conch filled with fresh butter,
there are four silver moon-stones and twelve Viṣṇupadas at the time of the sun’s passage into a new zodiac sign (saṃkrānti).
At the transits of Capricorn and Cancer, there are the northern and southern solstices respectively.
At the equinox, when the sun is at the center of the sphere, the other [parameters] follow from that.
The six signs beginning with Sagittarius—namely Sagittarius, Pisces, Aries, Taurus, Gemini, and Virgo—are designated as Ṣaḍaśīti;
likewise, Taurus, Scorpio, Aquarius, and Leo are designated as Viṣṇupadī.
One should know that from Cancer to Sagittarius is the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana),
and from Capricorn to Gemini is indeed the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa).
When the sun's transit occurs in Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Scorpio,
or Sagittarius, and [the month] has been lost, a double Āṣāḍha is prescribed.
When the sun enters [the signs] of Capricorn, Aquarius, Pisces, Aries,
Taurus, and Gemini, the wise man should observe a fast for two days.
There are sixteen *ghaṭikās* of meritorious time, both before and after the transit (*saṃkrama*). If the transit occurs immediately after midnight, the subsequent day indeed bestows merit.
If this should occur at midnight when the sun's transit is complete, [it is a special case].

Then, even if it is accompanied by two *ādina*s, or if it is contradictory (*viruddha*), or even if it is retrograde (*viloma*), the *puṣpa* [yoga] certainly effects the accomplishment of all desired goals, provided that the *pāṇigraha* [yoga] is excluded.
Thus ends the section on the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*).

In this system, those yogas associated with adverse designations (viruddhasaṃjñā) indeed bring about undesirable results, misfortune, and sin; however, the entire vaidhṛti yoga brings satisfaction, while even the whole of parigha is undesirable.
In the first yoga, Vajra, three nāḍīs must be avoided; in Vyāghāta, nine; in Śūla, five; and in Gaṇḍa, six nāḍīs are to be shunned for auspicious undertakings.
Thus ends the section on yoga.
Curd, sandalwood, water known as *samyākhyata*, white mustard seeds, and *rocanā*—these [are the substances].
One should prepare oil-cake sandalwood for the sake of accomplishing one's purpose in the rites involving substances and the like.
Whatever specific rite is prescribed for the day of a particular planet, all of that is likewise ordained for its *kālahorā*.
Thus ends the section on the days of the week.
In the two solstices and the two equinoxes, there are four [degrees] joined with six *aśīs*.
Jupiter has three and a half *nāḍīs* joined with seven *palas*; Venus has four [degrees] and one *pala*.
Two nāḍīs and seven palas are declared to be the meritorious [measure] for Saturn.
Whatever is given even without faith, to those who are immature,
or by men at an improper time— all that, being performed with sincerity, shall attain inexhaustibility.

Ghorārāvā occurs when the Sun is in transit; Amṛtadyuti when Mars is in transit; Mahodarī when Saturn is in transit; Mandākinī when Mercury or Jupiter is in transit; Miśrā when Venus is in transit; and Rākṣasikā when Rāhu is in transit.
The sun's transits through the constellations known as Ugra, Kṣipracara, Maitra, Dhruva, and Miśra are fierce and terrible; such is the sequence of its movements.

From a Vaiśya, a Dhvāṅkṣī gives birth to one who brings happiness, great pride, and a caravan of thieves; from a Śūdra, a Ghorā gives birth to one who is not at all satisfied; and from a Brāhmaṇa, a Mandākinī gives birth to a Mandā. Furthermore, from the group of excellent twice-born men, a Miśrakā gives birth to animals and Cāṇḍālas.
And the entire nature designated as "rakṣasī" (demoness).
In the forenoon, [one should perform] meritorious acts such as bathing and giving gifts.
Vṛhaspati.
In the northern course there are twenty [degrees] for the former [period], and twenty for the latter in Capricorn.
In the present [solar months] of Libra and Aries, there is no night-water; in both, it is ten [muhūrtas].
When eighty-six [nāḍīs] have elapsed, the sixth nāḍī is said to be meritorious; in the case of Viṣṇupadī, sixteen [nāḍīs] before and after [the moment of transition] are likewise auspicious.
If the transit occurs before midnight, the rites are performed after midday;
if it occurs after [midnight], they are performed for two watches (praharas) after sunrise.
If the sun enters a new sign exactly at midnight, they say that the period of two days is meritorious; this applies to both Capricorn and Cancer, which fulfill all desires.
In the case of Capricorn and Cancer, however, even at night, the time is meritorious according to its own established rule.
At the transit of the sun into a zodiacal sign, the constellations and signs are auspicious for three *nāḍīs* before and after;
likewise, for the moon, they are auspicious for two *nāḍīs* and one *nāḍī* minus sixty *pala*s, as declared by the wise.
For Mars, there are four fruitful channels; for Mercury, thirty; and for Jupiter and the Moon, eleven.
And by Guru and Bhārgava, the growth of the harvest is produced.
When the sun enters [a sign] on a Saturday or a Tuesday,
there will be famine, great upheaval, and even total destruction.
The fruit of the Viṣṇupadī is one hundred thousand multiplied by nine crores;
however, the wise have declared that the fruit of the Ṣaḍaśīti is one thousand six hundred.
Thus ends the section on transmigration.

They say that the three seasons beginning with Śiśira constitute the northern course (uttarāyaṇa), during which the day becomes immortal; the other three seasons are the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana), and that is declared to be the night of the gods.

Entering a house, entering a new dwelling, consecration, marriage, shaving, and the binding of the sacred thread—these rites should be performed during the northern solstice (saumyāyana) as they are auspicious; however, those actions which are forbidden should indeed be done during the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana).
From the Sun’s transit through two zodiac signs beginning with Capricorn, there are six seasons:
Śiśira, Vasanta, Grīṣma, Varṣā, Śarat, and likewise the sixth is said to be named Hemanta.
At midday he [should give] to kings and the best of the twice-born; at the afternoon hour to the Vaiśyas; at the eighth part of the day to the Śūdras;
and at nightfall to the Piśācas who roam at night; at midnight to the ghosts.

At the time of the latter part of the night and at dawn, it destroys actors and the like, as well as cattle-herders; and when the sun enters a new sign (saṃkrānti), it destroys all those bearing sectarian marks (liṅgin) at the time of twilight.
When the Sun enters [the zodiacal sign] while Catuṣpada, Ettila, and Nāga are asleep, it is a transit; likewise, when he is situated in Vidyā, Cāvākhye, Gatāṅka, Savālavākhye, and Valija.
However, O sages, when the sun is situated at the half-point during the *saṅkrānti* occurring in the *tithis* named Kiṃstughna and Kaulava,
the price of grain increases; the ancient seers declare that these results are respectively inauspicious and middling.

When the Sun enters a new sign on a Saturday, Tuesday, or Sunday, one should know that it is inauspicious for those [signs] due to wind, fire, and the king's hand. There is abundance of food, security, and health when it is in the domain of Varuṇa; therefore, the strength or weakness of the Moon is essential in all respects.
Where stars are not counted and where the moon is surpassed in splendor;
even when the Lord is not pleased, joy and anger are rendered motionless.

When Kṛṣṇa (the dark fortnight) is powerful, Tārā (the moon) is powerful; and when Śukla (the bright fortnight) is powerful, the Moon is powerful. Therefore, one should undertake an undertaking only when both the Moon and the stars are completely pure.

From the latter half of the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the former half of the eighth day of the bright fortnight, the moon of sin wanes; during the bright fortnight, it increases, and the opposite occurs during the dark fortnight.
When the moon has entered the bright half of the month (śuklapakṣa) and is situated in white-colored constellations such as Aśvinī and others, they declare it to be auspicious.
When it is in the dark half of the month (kṛṣṇapakṣa), it is inauspicious; however, if the dark half itself is unfavorable, then these two [halves] are considered the opposite.
The Moon in the ninth, second, fifth, or seventh house is considered by the wise to possess an increasing body;
it yields results similar to those of the minister of the gods.

In auspicious activities such as journeys and marriages, if the Moon has entered the hands of malefic planets and is devoid of strength, it causes manifold obstacles until the end of the month; they say that month is lunar (cāndra), while the solar (saura) month is measured by the Sun's transit through a zodiac sign,
and the Śāvana month consists of thirty days.
They say that the lunar mansion is called *saṃjñā*, and the circle of the moon is called *bhagaṇa*.
The solar month is prescribed for marriage and similar occasions; the Śrāvaṇa (lunar) month is prescribed for sacrifices and the like;
and the lunar month is prescribed for ancestral rites performed on auspicious occasions.
Madhu and Mādhava, Śukra and Śuci, then Nabhas and Nabhasya; likewise Iṣa and Ūrja, Sahas and Sahasya, and Tapas and Tapasya—these are enumerated in order.

The months and fortnights also have lords identical to those of their own names and constellations; both the fortnights of the gods and the ancestors are explained as being respectively the bright and the dark, and they are proclaimed to be auspicious or inauspicious for ritual actions.
Thus ends the section on months.
The lunar day (tithi) is said to have one quality, the weekday (vāra) has four qualities,
the asterism (ṛkṣa) sixteen qualities, and the yoga has more than a hundred qualities.
The Moon possesses a hundred thousand times the qualities of the Sun;
even when devoid of [beneficial] aspects, it bestows auspicious results if it is in its own or an exaltation sign, or if it is aspected by a strong Mercury that is its friend.
The nine divisions of the [planetary] states— birth, excellence,
opposition, enemy, neutral, means, wealth, friend, and over-friend— arise from these [positions].
The first is to be known as the bestower of success, the second as the cause of increase, the third as the giver of death,
and the fourth as the source of happiness and prosperity.
The fifth [tithi] bestows sorrow, the sixth is death, the sixth [again] accomplishes all aims; the seventh is full of disease, while the eighth brings joy and happiness.
The fruit resulting from honoring a Navamī Rājā Tārā has been proclaimed.
Just as the passage of the sun, garlanded with rays of frost, occurs through the sharp-rayed [sun],
so too does a person obtain a fruit corresponding to the cold-rayed moon’s power, whether it be good or bad.
The moon is said to transfer its power to Tārāvalā, and the sun to transfer its power to Rathendu;
furthermore, by the power of the sun, all planets— even those that are inauspicious— soon become highly auspicious for men.

The *puṃsavana* rite, the building of a house, the taking of a wife, and likewise the departure [on a journey]— these are not desired when the Moon is in a sign of sleep, nor when the Sun, Saturn, Mars, and the others are there.
If the Moon, occupying any of the seven houses from a malefic, is conjoined with or aspected by a malefic, one should avoid it;
this fault is declared to be certain.
It brings poison on a journey, death in the home, disease through a razor, and widowhood in marriage.
The Gaṇas [bring] death with pain for men at every step.
The Moon, when auspicious, bestows desired results when situated in the third (3), sixth (6), seventh (7), tenth (10), or eleventh (11) house from birth;
however, one should avoid it in the fourth (4), eighth (8), or twelfth (12) house, as it causes the loss of wealth and brings about disease and other afflictions.
The Moon, whether situated in its own house or that of a friend, or when aspected by a friend, illuminates the quarters with its stainless light;
having removed the defects of its friends, the Moon indeed brings about the desired fruit for human beings.

When the Moon is situated in an undesirable place, there is blindness at night; Gemini and Virgo possess the scent of a swarm of bees; Libra, Scorpio, and Sagittarius belong to the deaf; and Capricorn and Pisces occur during the evening twilight and the final hour for one who is humpbacked. [The result].

If the ascendant is one that causes blindness by day, women become widows; if it is one that causes blindness by night, there is loss of wealth. For the deaf, the continuity of the ascendant leads to the destruction of all possessions; thus it is said in the Jyotiṣa.
Disputes, the consecration of a king, acts of violence,
matters concerning agriculture, mines, and so forth, as well as whatever is declared regarding the sign of Taurus.
Rituals such as adorning oneself with ornaments and so forth should be performed at the rising of a *mithuna* (the Gemini sign).
In Cancer, all nourishing rites (pauṣṭika-karma), as well as the consecration of ponds, wells, tanks, and temples, are successfully accomplished.
Trade and so forth, the practice of incantations, agriculture, service to the king,
union with others, and the act of a lion— these are the deeds of Aries.
The knowledge of medicine and craftsmanship is established in the movement of the ornaments and so forth.
One should perform all auspicious rites during three lifetimes; however, one should avoid disputes, ancestral offerings (*śrāddha*), medical treatments, journeys, and shaving.

Excluding the eye and the non-active [planets], whatever other activity is desired— whether it be nourishing (*pauṣṭika*), auspicious (*maṅgalya*), victorious (*jaya*), or a journey (*yātrā*)— is sought even in the activity of the birth asterism (*janmakṣa*).

Agriculture, building a house, marriage, sacrifices, the investiture of the sacred thread, coronations, the beds of young women, garments, perfumes, and ointments— whatever else has been described as auspicious for all rites, O noble ones, you conclude that these do not yield favorable results here when one is born under a *janmabhē* (natal asterism).

On a journey there will be obstruction on the road; in agricultural work, the loss of all one's wealth; likewise, death from medicine; in the construction of a house, a burning fever; in shaving, the onset of various diseases; in the offering of funeral cakes (śrāddha), the loss of wealth;
and in trade, the destruction of intelligence or the fear of war.
In the birth ascendant.
Thus ends the section on the moon and stars.
In Kaṇḍiraka, Vṛṣa, Rāśi, Divādi, and so forth, these aforementioned actions are accomplished;
however, when these are afflicted by the aspect or conjunction of malefic planets, the undertaking of those actions will indeed be fierce.
The ascendant, horā, drekkāṇa, navāṃśa, dvādaśāṃśa, and triṃśāṃśa constitute the sixfold division (ṣaḍvarga); when produced by benefic planets, it is auspicious.

When the lord of the varga is in an auspicious sign and the Lagna is occupied by a benefic, such nourishing rites (pauṣṭika) are prescribed by the wise. Furthermore, if the Lagna is occupied by a malefic planet, there will be success for the most cruel act of ploughing (karṣaṇa).
Aquarius, Gemini, Cancer, Aries, Taurus, and Virgo are the auspicious signs here; these seven are the houses of the benefics.
Scorpio, Aquarius, Capricorn, Leo, and Aries are declared by the sages to be the houses of the malefics, according to their respective natures.
The malefic houses.
The mildness of these planets is indeed not by their very nature; rather, it arises from their conjunction with others.

Among the planets, even a malefic becomes mild when associated with a benefic, while a benefic becomes fierce when associated with a malefic. Auspicious rites for prosperity should be undertaken when the ascendant is Cancer, for success is achieved in that position.
Just as in the case of agriculture or trade, here too, actions are successful when they are undertaken with effort and depend upon profit.

One should perform the *sāhasa* (impetuous), *dākuṇa* (deceptive), and *ugra* (fierce) rites during the *rājasa* (passionate) period; likewise, the *cauryakarma* (acts of theft) should be performed when the moon is in the *raṃbhā* (kanyā) asterism, and the *vṛścika* (scorpion) rite during the *udaya* (rising) period.
Departure, nourishing rites, marriage, massage, and acquisition should be performed in the sign of Sagittarius for the sake of success, as well as wandering and other such activities.

During the rising of Capricorn (makarodaye), one should undertake agricultural work, journeys, the binding and releasing of water, the acquisition of female slaves, quadrupeds such as camels and the like, and other such tasks.
The practice of the lower vehicle, the water-vehicle, and likewise the performance of constant ritual acts, as well as the gathering and sowing of seeds, should be performed at the rising of the jar.
The wise should perform activities such as the arts of perfumery and jewelry-making, agriculture,
the tending of cattle, processions, marriages, and consecrations during the rising of Pisces.
In pure signs such as Aries and the like, the Moon is not auspicious even when situated in the ascendant and conjoined with benefics; nor is the ascendant itself auspicious for death.
Having first determined the strength for all [planets] when they are in conjunction, the Moon's strength is then considered different;
when the cool-rayed one (the Moon) possesses strength, all the lords of the planets become strong.
The *ādhāra* is the *bala-sūkta* of the Moon, while the *ādheya* is the power (*vīrya*) born of the planets;
these are established upon the *ādhāra-śakti*, for it is within the object to be supported that powers truly reside.
Just as all these celestial bodies, relying on the seed of the nectar-rayed moon's potency, bestow their respective fruits—whether good or bad—upon their own particular domains;
so too, the senses, when presided over by the mind alone, become attached to their own objects like flowers.
Those [houses] which are described as being either in contact with or not in contact with the Ascendant—the lord of the planets situated in them bestows the results pertaining to the Ascendant.
That [planet] which has passed beyond them becomes associated with the second house; one should apply this same principle to the remaining positions. Thus it is said.
If there is no benefic planet in the tenth house from the ascendant or from the Moon, or if the lord of the birth sign is not in the tenth house during a journey,
the teachers say that it is not auspicious.
When the planets are near the end of their [respective] orbits, the state of the zodiacal sign follows; the planet follows;
then, when freed from that, the planet reverts to its own inherent nature.
In the beginning, a lagna that bestows a complete fruit; in the middle, one that yields a middling fruit;
and at the end, one whose fruit is exceedingly meager—this is the conclusion esteemed by the wise.
When the Moon is situated in a cruel division of a malefic planet and is devoid of strength,
one should indeed perform the *ahicāra* rite for the destruction of misfortune (*riṣṭa*) in those yogas.
When the Moon is situated in the sign of Sagittarius, there is complete purification through expenditure and fuel, the arising of right view,
and success in all undertakings.
By Śaktiśālī, Niṣiteśa, Śītagau, Durvala, Asita, Bhauma, and Bhāskara.
When Jupiter is situated in the ascendant, like the moon, there is the arising of lotuses; [likewise], when it is in the ascendant, agricultural work prospers.

Generally, the houses of the eighth and twelfth, as well as those presided over by the lords of the ninth, twelfth, and fifth, and those situated in the second house or the quadrants (kendras), are said to grant auspicious results. The *sarvārthasiddhi*, *hādhviloka*, *agraha*, *loka*, and *aloka* yogas are declared to occur in the ascendant and its dimensions, both in direct and reverse order.

In the first *lagna*, Aries, Sagittarius, Capricorn, and Virgo are the "first-footed" (*ādipāda*) signs; Taurus, Leo, Cancer, Scorpio, and Aquarius are the "arm-crawlers" (*bhujanga*); Leo, Aquarius, Libra, and Gemini are the "middle" (*madhyama*) signs; and Pisces and Virgo are the "slow-moving" (*mṛdhrasaṃjña*) signs.
The Yavanas, speakers of untruth, do not honor the lunar day, nor the asterism, nor the weekday, nor even the planetary mansion; they honor only the *lagna*.
Thus ends the section on the Ascendant (Lagna).
All planets are auspicious when situated in the eleventh house; the Sun is auspicious in the third, sixth, and tenth; Mars and Saturn in the third, sixth, and tenth;
the Moon in the third, sixth, tenth, and seventh; Jupiter in the third, sixth, tenth, fifth, ninth, and twelfth; and Mercury in the fourth, sixth, tenth, and eighth houses.
If [the planet] is not found in another house, it should be known that even though situated in an auspicious [house], the planets become [malefic].
The Sun is subtracted from the [mean] Moon by five, two, twelve, nine, and zero;
the Moon is subtracted from the [mean] Sun by five, nine, two, eight, and thirty-three.

Twelve, five, and four and a half [nakṣatras] from the Sun and Moon; Mars and Saturn [occupy] the refuge (śaraṇya), wood (kāṣṭha), and the end of the sin (aghamanta); Mercury is divided by one, two, and eight [nakṣatras].
Ten days, half a day, three-quarters of a day, two-tenths of a day, and one-thirtieth of a day— thus he declared the strengths of the vargas, each subsequent one being stronger than the preceding.

If the Sun and Moon are situated in the eighth house (Nidhana), there will be loss of wealth and destruction of one's home. However, if a malefic planet is in the eighth house, there will be various kinds of diseases and piercing pain.
Indeed, through a multitude of virtues acquired over even a few days, a great abundance of merit and a high regard for it arise,
while defects become insignificant; for in this world, a defect cannot prevail against a vast accumulation of virtues, just as a single drop of water cannot prevail against a large fire.

In this world, even a single fault can overwhelm a hundred thousand virtues; yet if a certain other quality exists, it is not opposed to that [fault]. Even a single drop of wine defiles a jar full of pure cow's milk.
The Sun has seven eyes, and the Moon has nine paths as its eyes; the three voids are the worlds, and the earth is the foremost ground of the worlds of the paths.
Jupiter and Venus are the two entries, while Saturn and the Moon are the two exits; Mercury, however, bestows all fruits.
Whichever zodiacal sign the planets occupy and through which they move by aspect, in that very sign the planets— whether in retrograde or other motions— shall bestow their results.
When the lords of the planets have moved into their respective *krānticāra* positions, they bestow their fruits upon those situated therein—
both undesirable and desirable results for men— whether it be Mars or others, during travel, marriage, or the birth of a son.

House construction should be performed when the Sun is auspicious; religious vows and marriage when both the Sun and Jupiter are auspicious; shaving when both the lunar asterism and the Moon are auspicious;
and all other matters should be determined according to the Moon.
The Sun is powerful during the inspection of the king; Jupiter during the marriage; Mars during the wearing of ornaments; the son of Bhṛgu (Venus) during the journey;
Saturn during the moment of casting a glance; Mercury during all scriptural studies; and the Moon is certainly declared by the wise to be powerful in all actions.
If the Sun is situated in an inauspicious sign, it is defeated by a planet when it is in the eighth, second, third, or twelfth house from a benefic;
likewise, if Venus is situated in the seventh, twelfth, or fourteenth house, it is defeated.

Whatever fruit is to be given by a planet for attaining an auspicious state is not realized if that planet is eclipsed by another planet, just as the fruit of a sacrifice does not reach its goal when the deity is absent.
O Sage, it has been declared by the sages that if a planet is situated in its sign of debilitation or is set, the results of the planets become entirely fruitless.
When pierced by these [aspects], all the planets within their respective spheres become fruitless;
however, when pierced in the reverse manner, even malefic planets should be known as auspicious.
A planet that yields an inauspicious result when aspected by a benefic, yet bestows auspicious results when aspected by a malefic—
both of these two lords of celestial bodies become fruitless if they are aspected by their own enemy.
One who abides here in the royal household should avoid wandering at improper times, hunting, rashness, riding on difficult vehicles, mounting elephants or horses, and entering the houses of others.
With saffron, uśīra, yaṣṭimadhu, and lotuses combined together;
When the sun is situated in an unfavorable position, bathing with *śataprapuṣpa* flowers is declared by the wise to bring auspiciousness.

This bath, prescribed for kings, consists of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) mixed with elephant secretions, along with conch shells, pearl oysters, white water-lilies, and crystal; it destroys the afflictions caused by the cool-rayed moon.
They say that bathing with bilva, sandalwood, aruṇa flowers, hiṅgulūka, phalinī, and bakula flowers, along with māṃsī, wards off the afflictions caused by Mars.
This bath with cow dung, unbroken rice, fruits, yellow pigment (*rocanā*), honey, oyster shells, *ūmūla*,
and gold is declared by the wise to be for the nourishment of beings and the destruction of inauspiciousness through the recitation of mantras.
Water mixed with jasmine flowers, white mustard seeds, sprouts from the *madayantī* plant,
and *madhuka*, clearly cuts away even severe deformities caused by [demonic] influence.

If the waters are endowed with *elayā* and *gilayā*, it will be auspicious for fish and conch shells; having abandoned [the prediction] for thirteen days, one should declare the remainder to be favorable (*bhadra*).
Mars [rules] these fifteen [years], and Mercury [rules] more than that.
Vāgīśa [Jupiter] has eight months, Niśākara [the Moon] one day, and Manda [Saturn] one month;
the year-long transit is nine years less a quarter.
As long as it remains fully risen, so long shall the fire-god bestow its fruit.

Coral should be worn for the sake of contentment by one born on Tuesday; silver for those born on Friday and Monday; gold for one born on Thursday; pearl for one born on Saturday; iron for one born on Sunday; and rājāvarta is prescribed for those born on the remaining two days (Wednesday and Monday).
A pure, high-quality ruby for the Sun; a pearl for the Moon; coral for Mars; an emerald for Mercury;
a topaz for Jupiter; a diamond for Venus; a flawless sapphire for Saturn; and for the other two [Rāhu and Ketu], a gem of their own kind.
When Gomedaka and Vaidūrya are mentioned.
Covered with realgar, cardamom, and suradā, they are auspicious and measure one span in length.
For success, one should employ *viguṇa* when the Sun is [the lord], *ravīśa* for the Moon, *śadharī* for Mars, *rodhra* and *haridrā* for Mercury, likewise *kujamūsta* for Jupiter,
*māṃsī* and *mūśīla* for Venus, *mārtaṇḍī*, *phalinī*, *vañcā*, *asuraridha*, *dhānya*, and *dhūmadhvaja* for Saturn. For longevity, these are the [remedies].
One whose mind is uplifted by the auspicious increase of prosperity should always perform the sacrifice for the sake of purification.
A cow, a conch, a bull with a reddish luster, gold, yellow cloth, a white horse, a fragrant black goat, and black iron—
these are declared by the sages to be the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) for the Sun and the other planets, following ritual baths, gifts, and oblations.
For they are satisfied by the rituals performed therein.
Thus ends the section on the planets.
Now, the results according to the houses (bhāvas).

A man born under the Sun (Savitṛ) is afflicted by diseases in his youth, suffers greatly from eye ailments, and is devoted to service. He does not become a householder, is beset by wretchedness, and wanders about with his very roots and foundation shattered. However, through bathing with saffron (*kuṅkuma*) offered by the son of Bhṛgu (Śukra), the suffering he has incurred undergoes dissolution; of this there is no doubt.
With black sesame seeds, *nalada*, *lodhra*, and *balā*, combined with *śatakusumā*, agaru, and parched grain (*lāja*),
this bath for the head and other parts of the body, declared by the Son of the Sun (Śanaiścara), removes the misfortunes of one situated in an unfavorable planetary position.
Just as diseases are destroyed by hundreds of medicinal herbs and sorrows and fears are dispelled by mechanical devices,
so too, through the performance of the prescribed bathing rite as it has been described, the inauspicious influence of the planets reaches an indescribable destruction.
Kuṣṭha, māṃsī, haridrā, mūla, śaileya, campaka,
vacā, akuru, mustā, and elā— this is called the "all-herbs" (sarvauṣadhi) collection.

For the purpose of the fire-oblation (homa) for the circle of planets beginning with the Sun, wise men should prepare sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) from the following trees in order: Arka, Brāhmī, Mahīruha, Khadira, Apāmārga, Pippala, Ādityavara-śākhi, Śamī, Durvā, and Kuśa.
[Fuel] that is very glossy and straight produces a single son.
One who possesses wealth and hands, is brave, yet has a cowardly mind, is a dandy, performs cruel deeds, and is poorly dressed. || 5 ||
When the Sun is in Atigṛhaṇata, one becomes devoted to yoga, wise, a benefactor to his own family, and a source of joy to his circle of kinsmen;
though thin-bodied, he is a householder of beautiful form, playful, a conqueror of enemies, honored for his deeds, and firm of limb. (6)
When [the Moon] is situated in the house of horses (the seventh house), the Sun becomes a lover of women, powerful, fortunate, fickle, and of sinful character;
he has a body that is neither emaciated nor fat, is of moderate height—neither too tall nor too short—and possesses brown eyes, a reddish-brown complexion, and a small physique. || 7 ||

When the Sun is in the eighth house, the native is impetuous, generous by nature, and well-served by physicians; yet he is always afflicted by disease, speaks much that is false, is considered unfortunate, lacks moral conduct, is devoid of pleasure, is poorly dressed, addicted to women, and lives abroad.
The lord of the day (the Sun) situated in a planet [house] makes one truthful in speech, yet devoid of sons and wife. || 1 ||
If the Sun is situated in the second house (the house of wealth), a man becomes devoid of sons and gifts, emaciated in body, extremely dejected, with blood-red eyes, and of wicked conduct.
He is truly joined with poverty, possesses no gold or copper, does not remain a householder, and becomes a partaker of suffering.
If the Sun is situated in the third house, he causes the destruction of brothers, acts for the welfare of dear ones, and is occupied with his sons and wife.
And thus, endowed with such virtues, possessed of fortitude, patient, enjoying vast wealth, he brings joy to his mother. (3)
When the Sun is situated in Dhanavihāri, a person becomes possessed of various kinds of wealth and kin, gentle-minded, and devoted to song and instrumental music.
In battle at the forefront of combat, there is no defeat whatsoever; he possesses abundant wealth and a wife, and is beloved by kings.

If Saturn is in the fifth house, one does not experience suffering regarding children, nor does one become a possessor of wealth; rather, one is afflicted by disease in youth and is fearful. Thus ends the results of the Sun.
If the Moon is in its own sign or exaltation, the native will have a slender body, possess wealth, be virtuous, enjoy the company of many people, be endowed with valor, and have a beautiful physique;
however, if the Moon is in its fall, he will be devoid of wealth, possess a dull intellect, and be exceedingly wretched. || 1 ||
When the Moon is in the second house, one is generous by nature, wise, full of wealth like a treasure-trove, yet fickle-minded and highly joyful.
He produces much happiness, possesses a face like a blooming lotus, and his beauty is equal to the moon.
(1) When the Moon is situated in its own house but in a sign of malefic planets, it is true that he does not possess great fortune; he becomes a killer of his wife and is extremely foolish. (2)
And he becomes a partaker of happiness, O gentle lord of the night, a treasury of all virtues, and one who finds delight in poetry and the sciences. || 3 ||

O Lord, when Rātrinātha (the Moon) is present, one will be filled with abundant pleasures, be intent on the welfare of his beloved wife, bring joy to women, possess beautiful hair, and act for the benefit of his noble kin;
he will be devoted to gods and Brahmins, be somewhat sickly in early youth, yet endowed with the stability of youth, a possessor of great wealth, and long-lived.
Sumurtiḥ || 9 ||

When the Sun is situated in the tenth house, men enjoy abundant happiness and prosperity; they are charitable, virtuous, and dignified, gentle, pure, and moderate in eating; they are devoted to dance and song, are honored like a king, fulfill their remaining duties, yet remain subject to illness.

One who occupies the house of the Sun in the Ayasaṃstha yoga becomes a possessor of vast wealth, yet is devoid of enjoyment; he is a connoisseur of virtues, lean of body, and excessively passionate. He is a stealer of women's wealth, fickle-minded, and finds delight among his circle of kinsmen.

When the Sun is situated in the twelfth house, one becomes dull-witted, excessively lustful, a dallyer with the wives of others, a destroyer of flocks of birds, evil-minded, and of ugly form; even if possessed of wealth, he is antagonistic toward storytellers and suffers from diseases of the legs.
However, if that Sun is in its own house, in the house of a malefic, or in the houses of Venus, Jupiter, or Mercury, it produces a full life.

When the cool-rayed Moon is situated in the ninth house, there is much suffering from diseases such as *kāśa* and *pitta*. However, when it is full, one acquires abundant wealth, speaks pleasantly, and brings joy to women. When it is waning or in its sign of debilitation (*nicarāśi*), one does not enjoy wealth, lacks vigor, and is blocked from the path of purity, becoming destitute.
One whose mind is deluded. || 9 ||
When the Moon is situated in the tenth house (the house of action), one speaks with great wealth, becomes a treasury of various virtues, and is filled with sons and gifts; however,
when it is in an enemy sign or a crooked house (the third or sixth), one suffers from consumption, has a lean body, is wealthy through paternal women, yet is devoid of professional success.
A human being. || 10 ||
When the Moon is situated in the fourth house, one partakes of many pleasures, possesses abundant sons, and is endowed with a wife, servants, and so forth.
However, when the Moon is weak in body and conjoined with malefic planets, one does not enjoy happiness;
rather, being constantly afflicted by disease here on earth and greedy for fish and meat, he sports in his palace with snakes.
On the back. || 4 ||
If the Moon is situated in the eleventh house, one will be full of wealth, happy, endowed with abundant riches, and accompanied by beautiful women; however,
if the Moon is in the fifth house in a sign of diminished strength or an inimical sign, it destroys the mass of happiness for kings.
The Moon situated in an enemy’s house, or one that is waned, in its sign of debilitation, or in an inimical sign, bestows unhappiness and is a giver of the suffering of disease.
However, if the Moon is in its own house, its exaltation, or possesses a full orb, it will be a giver of abundant happiness.
Of the kings. || 6 ||

When the Moon of pure form is situated in the seventh house, the husband of a woman is wise, handsome, youthful, and wealthy in gold; however, if the Moon is afflicted by a malefic planet or aspected by a malefic while its body is emaciated, he does not become a speaker of pleasant words, nor does he remain the husband of a woman born under Rohiṇī.
Together.
The Moon situated in the eighth house causes men to experience physical suffering; however, if it is in its exaltation or in a sign of Mars, the person becomes playful and enjoys pleasures.
If it is in its fall, in an inimical house, or in an utterly wretched house, one becomes destitute of wealth and happiness.

If Mars is situated in the *jātra* (the seventh house from the lord of the ascendant), being exceedingly weak and associated with kinsmen, the wife of the family becomes destitute of relatives and suffers in misery.
In the region of Bhavati-maśaka, one will be devoted to the service of the lowly, dependent on the wealth and wives of others, and possess a mind that seeks only meager enjoyments. || 4 ||
If Mars is situated in the house of children, a man becomes blind, destitute of wealth, and exceedingly miserable;
however, if Mars is in its own exaltation, he will give birth to one son whose mind is devoted to religious duty.
When Mars has gone to the house of an enemy, one suffers death in battle; yet when situated in the portion of Mercury, one stands possessed of abundant sons and wealth.
When the Son of the Earth (Mars) is afflicted by a host of enemies or is in its sign of debilitation, one becomes deficient, diseased, foolish, and insane.
If the Moon is situated in the eighth house, one becomes wealthy; if it is in the eleventh house, one is a lord of the earth with vast lands and endowed with sons, daughters, and other blessings.
If the Moon is in the twelfth house, one has a lean body; if it is in the sixth house, one possesses little physical comfort and suffers from disease due to association with base people.
Thus ends the results of the Moon.

If Mars is in the *lagna* during childhood, the person suffers from diseases of the stomach and teeth; he is malicious-minded, has a deformed body, is afflicted by phlegmatic disorders and leprosy, possesses a fickle mind, is of low intelligence, poorly dressed, devoid of all happiness, and is habitually engaged in every kind of sin. || 1 ||
When Mars is situated in the second house (the house of wealth), the person is a traveler for the sake of wealth, preoccupied with debts and riches, a gambler, and patient.
He is capable of farming, possesses little wealth despite his valor, has a lean body, and always experiences only moderate happiness.
When Mars is situated in the third house, he is a slayer of his brothers, emaciated, yet endowed with fortitude and strength.
The red [color] is for the sake of those desiring merit and wealth. || 11 ||
When Mars is situated in the twelfth house, one desires to seize the wealth of others, is always stingy, fickle in conduct, fond of jesting, and fierce;
he does not partake in happiness, yet he dallies with the wives of others and is engaged in secret deeds.
The Hero.
Thus ends the results of Mars.
When Mercury is situated in the third house, one will possess a radiant body and great joy, be highly intelligent, virtuous, and learned;
he will be pure, gentle, clean-eating, truthful, playful, a benefactor to his family, and a source of delight for refined women. || 1 ||
When the son of the Moon (Mercury) is situated in the second house, one becomes truthful, playful, fortunate in wealth, and constantly traveling abroad;
he is devoted to his father, handsome, possesses a wife who is sinful, has soft skin and sparse body hair, and is fair-complexioned with long limbs. (2)

When Mercury is situated in the house of the elder brother, the person possesses an appearance filled with abundant wealth, yet is gluttonous and sinful; he has many wives and a full household while his house is in its ascendant state.
His intellect is fickle, his shanks are emaciated, his body is thin, and he suffers from disease during childhood.
In the mansion of the virtuous, the son of the Moon (Mercury) makes one a recipient of happiness, endowed with children and a wife;
he possesses a face like a blooming lotus, is a poet, is auspicious, and has devotion and a mind fixed upon the preceptor of the gods and the twice-born (Brahmins). || 4 ||
He dwelt in the house of a courtesan; he was contemptible and of cruel deeds.

When Mars is situated in the house of a sage (the fifth house), he bestows upon men the suffering of being separated from their young wives. When the lord [of the ascendant] is in its own Capricorn house, he gives a wife who is fickle-minded, deformed, evil-natured, and broad-hipped. (7)

When Mars is situated in the eighth house, being waned and debilitated, a man enters the state of death; afflicted by extremely harsh phlegm, hiccups, dysentery, and other diseases of the hands and feet, he departs for the world of the dead.

If the Moon is situated in the ninth house from the *savana-lagna*, the person will have a son, yet be afflicted by disease; his eyes and body will be tawny (*piṅgala*), and his entire physique will be so.
He will possess abundant water and wealth, yet be devoid of fortune (*bhāgya*); he will wear dirty clothes, be fond of pure people, and be devoted to limited knowledge.
One who has lost his wealth in the tenth house is deceitful, lacking in treasury, yet causes fear to his family; he captivates the hearts of women.
His body is like his belly, he lives off the earth, is irascible, devoted to Brahmins, elders, and gods, and is neither too tall nor too short. || 10 ||
When Jupiter is situated in the seventh house, the householder becomes a benefactor to his wife, like a king; he is wise yet prone to anger.
When Jupiter is in the eighth house, he brings about good fortune for the world.
The same results as those stated for Jupiter are also declared for Mercury and Venus when they are in the eighth house.
Thus ends the results of Mercury.

A man becomes a poet, a fine singer, pleasant to behold, pure, a donor, an enjoyer, honored by kings, happy, devoted to the service of gods and brahmins, and wealthy, when Jupiter is situated in the body [the first house]. (1)
When Jupiter is in the second house, one is always delighted by prosperity, is ever fond of perfumes and garlands, and possesses pearls,
gold, and gems.
And when Jupiter is in Sahajamandira (the fourth house), one becomes endowed with wealth along with brothers;
yet he falls into a state of wretchedness, and even though possessed of wealth, he is like one who has lost everything.

When Jupiter has thus gone to the fourth house, the beloved of the people, stationed upon the chest of his friend [the Sun], the native is happy in a house made of gold and jewels, sporting with various garlands and excellent women. || 4 ||
When Jupiter, the preceptor of the gods, enters the house of Jupiter (the ninth house), a man becomes endowed with many sons, cattle, and wealth;
he possesses an intellect versed in extensive scriptures, becomes a vessel of happiness, and is pleasing in appearance to all people. || 5 ||
When Jupiter is in the seventh house, the enemy hosts are conquered by those who have entered the ocean of battle;
however, if Jupiter is retrograde in the seventh house, he then spreads fear among the enemy clans.
If Saturn is retrograde and situated in the house of women (the seventh), it brings wealth equal to the happiness of a king to the leader of the gods;

however, if it is in the house of enemies (the sixth), it causes fear from enemy forces. But if it is in the house of merit (the ninth) and aspected by benefics, it destroys the host of enemies and bestows auspiciousness. (5)
When Mercury is situated in the sixth house, it clearly bestows a body that is emaciated and devoid of strength;
one becomes wealthy through the property of another's wife, yet is addicted to tens of millions of vices and is full of curiosity and passion.
If the Moon is in the seventh house from the horse (the seventh sign from the Ascendant), one becomes a husband of a barren woman who is fickle on earth;
however, if the Moon is born in the lineage of Vidula, he becomes the husband of a beautiful woman. || 7 ||
If a benefic planet is situated in the eighth house (Nidhana), it bestows longevity; however, if it is joined with a malefic, it causes death in water at a sacred ford (Tīrtha).
Furthermore, if it is conjoined with a malefic and located in the sixth house, it results in injury to the mouth and throat, and destruction of pleasure.
If Mercury is endowed with the lord of the ninth house, the lord of the third house,
the Moon, Jupiter, and Venus, and is situated in a house of virtue (a benefic sign) rather than on an evil path, he brings delight to the Vedas.

A man who is not devoted to the welfare of his elders, yet possesses great wealth, with Venus as the lord of the tenth house and the Moon in the fifth, enjoys pleasures acquired by his own arms and speaks in various delightful ways. || 10 ||
When the Moon is in Āyagata-nandana, one becomes deceitful in intellect, miserly, emaciated yet possessing great wealth, beloved by women, with a handsome dark-complexioned body and large eyes. (11)
If Venus is situated in the ascendant, one is intent on appropriate expenditure and devoted to music; one finds delight in poetry and the sciences, and is righteous. (1)
One who is constantly wealthy through earnings from learning, or even one who possesses wealth from a wife's property,
may become prone to anger toward silver during the second sub-period of the son of Bhṛgu (Venus).
When Venus is situated in Sahama Mandira, one is joined with many brothers and sisters;
yet one becomes afflicted by eye diseases, possesses wealth, is always miserly, and is harsh.
When Venus has gone to the Ativandhu (the eighth house), the man is surrounded by many kinsmen and sons;
he delights in battle, dwells in the midst of happiness, and is endowed with the playful charms of excellent women.
When the son of Bhṛgu (Venus) is in the house of the son (the fifth house), one is honored by the wife of the son or daughter;
he becomes wealthy, virtuous, an excellent leader, and a beloved husband who delights in beautiful amorous play. || 5 ||
Even when Venus has set, it causes excessive enmity, quarrels, and diseases;
however, when situated in its exaltation or its friendly house, it always bestows strength, even when it is in the houses of its enemies.

He will be the husband of a woman born of a pure lineage, residing in a palace of young women; he will be endowed with many sons and wealth. His speech will be like a mass of nectar, he will be wise, handsome-faced, and beloved by women. (7)
And in the excellent holy place Vimalatīrtha, Jupiter always brings about the destruction of wealth and the instability of riches;
one who falls into this yoga-path is forever deprived of wealth and wife. (8)
In the ninth [position] from Jupiter, one becomes an excellent man, a pure ruler of the earth,
an expounder of various poetic compositions and stories, a bearer of celebrated fame, and beloved by women.

And when Jupiter is in the tenth house, there arises a righteous man who is the best among the wise, adorned with jewels and gems, victorious through the virtues of his policy, and having conquered his enemies. || 10 ||

He attains equality with the lord of the earth through his wealth, always bringing glory to his own lineage; devoted to all forms of righteousness, he remains ever-endowed with prosperity when the Moon enters the constellation Āyāgata (Jyeṣṭhā).
When Jupiter is situated in the twelfth house, the child becomes afflicted by disease, his face is constantly turned toward begging,
and he always brings distress to his family through deceitful conduct.
Thus ends the result of the Guru.
He was talkative like an artisan; he was a craftsman who was always possessed by the fever of his craft even when at leisure. || 1 ||
When [the Moon] is situated in the eighth house, it causes the accumulation of wood, iron, and base metals; one is devoted to low arts, miserable, and destitute of wealth.
